name: Verilog
year_note: First appeared in 1984 at Gateway Design Automation (date from Wikipedia, used as a pointer; the primary history paper at ACM could not be fetched). First IEEE standard: IEEE 1364-1995.
org: Gateway Design Automation, later Cadence; standardized by IEEE (1364), now merged into SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800)
typing: static, weak; values are bits and bit vectors with four states
runs: A simulator runs the description as events over time, or a synthesis tool turns it into a network of logic gates for a chip or FPGA.
what: Verilog is a hardware description language: instead of listing steps for a processor to follow, it describes the circuit itself, with wires, registers and logic that all act at the same time. Engineers use it to design and test digital chips before they are built. Its syntax borrows from C. The standard has since been merged into its successor, SystemVerilog.
used_for: Designing processors and other digital chips
Simulating and testing circuits before manufacture

name: VHDL
year_note: First IEEE standard, IEEE 1076-1987. Development began in 1983 under a US Air Force contract in the Department of Defense VHSIC program (dates from Wikipedia, used as a pointer).
designers: Team from Intermetrics, IBM and Texas Instruments
org: US Department of Defense VHSIC program; standardized by IEEE (1076)
typing: static, strong
runs: A simulator runs the description as concurrent processes over time, or a synthesis tool turns it into a network of logic gates for a chip or FPGA.
what: VHDL is a hardware description language. A VHDL file describes a digital circuit, its inputs, outputs and behavior, and tools either simulate that circuit or build it. It was created so that suppliers to the US military could document exactly how their chips behave. It takes most of its syntax and semantics from Ada.

name: Assembly language
year_note: Earliest known assembly-style notation: 'Coding for A.R.C.' by Andrew Booth and Kathleen Britten, 1947 (via Wikipedia, used as a pointer). Every processor family has its own assembly language.
org: None; each processor maker defines its own
typing: none; everything is bits in registers and memory
runs: An assembler translates each line more or less one for one into a machine instruction, and the processor executes those instructions directly.
what: Assembly language is a human-readable way of writing the instructions a processor actually executes. Each line names one small step, such as moving a number into a register or adding two registers. It is not one language but a family, one per processor design, such as x86-64 or AArch64. Almost nobody writes whole programs in it today, but compilers produce it and the fastest inner loops are still written by hand.
used_for: Boot code and the lowest layers of operating systems
Hand-tuned inner loops in video and cryptography code

.global _main
_main:
    mov   x0, #48
    mov   x1, #18
gcd: cbz   x1, done

    msub  x2, x2, x1, x0
    mov   x0, x1
    mov   x1, x2
    b     gcd
done: ret

name: WebAssembly
year_note: Browser vendors reached consensus on the first version on February 28, 2017; it became a W3C Recommendation on December 5, 2019.
org: W3C WebAssembly Community Group and Working Group
typing: static; every instruction and function has a checked type built from a few number types
runs: A compiler for another language produces a compact binary module, which a browser or other host validates and then compiles to the real processor's instructions inside a sandbox.
what: WebAssembly is an instruction set for a machine that does not physically exist: a virtual processor that every major browser implements. Programs in C, C++, Rust and other languages are compiled to it, so they can run on a web page at close to native speed and inside the browser's safety sandbox. It has a binary format for machines and a text format, shown here, for people. It is rarely written by hand.
used_for: Running C, C++ and Rust code in web browsers
Bringing large desktop applications to the web

(module
  (func $gcd (export "gcd") (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    (local $t i32)
    (block $done
      (loop $next
        (br_if $done (i32.eqz (local.get $b)))
        (local.set $t (i32.rem_u (local.get $a) (local.get $b)))
        (local.set $a (local.get $b))
        (local.set $b (local.get $t))
        (br $next)))
    (local.get $a)))

name: C
year_note: Developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs between 1972 and 1973 as a successor to B (dates from Wikipedia, which cites Ritchie's own history paper; the Bell Labs copy of the paper refused automated fetches).
org: Bell Labs; standardized by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 22/WG 14
typing: static, weak; the programmer manages memory by hand
runs: A compiler translates the source ahead of time into machine code for one kind of processor; there is no garbage collector and almost no runtime.
what: C is a small language that sits just above the machine. It was created at Bell Labs to build the Unix system and its utilities, and it gives the programmer direct access to memory through pointers while staying portable across processors. That mix of control and portability is why operating system kernels, databases and the interpreters of other languages are still written in it. The price is that memory mistakes are easy to make and the language does not catch them.

what: C++ started as C with classes added, an attempt to combine the speed of C with the program-organizing ideas of Simula. It lets programmers build high-level abstractions that compile down to code as fast as hand-written C. Browser engines, game engines and compilers are typical C++ programs.

name: Rust
year_note: 1.0 released May 15, 2015. The language began within Mozilla, and the independent Rust Foundation was formed in February 2021.
typing: static, inferred; ownership and borrowing are checked at compile time
runs: Compiled ahead of time to machine code, usually through LLVM; there is no garbage collector.
what: Rust is a systems language that aims for the speed and control of C and C++ without their memory bugs. Its compiler tracks who owns each piece of memory and rejects programs that could use memory after freeing it or share it unsafely between threads. That checking happens before the program runs, so there is no garbage collector slowing it down.

name: Zig
year_note: First public introduction by Andrew Kelley on February 8, 2016. There is no 1.0 yet; the latest release on ziglang.org is 0.17.1 (November 2, 2026).
typing: static; types are values that ordinary code can compute at compile time
runs: Compiled ahead of time to machine code; there is no garbage collector, and any function that allocates memory is handed an allocator explicitly.
what: Zig is a small systems language meant to do the jobs C does, in a more careful way. Its rule is that nothing is hidden: no hidden control flow, no hidden memory allocation, no preprocessor or macros. Code that must run at compile time is written in Zig itself. The Zig toolchain can also compile C and C++ and cross-compile to other systems out of the box.

name: Ada
year_note: Ada 83, the first standard. Designed from 1977 to 1983 under contract to the US Department of Defense (dates from Wikipedia, used as a pointer; the design team is named in the Ada Reference Manual).
org: CII Honeywell Bull for the US Department of Defense; now an ISO standard
typing: static, strong; ranges and other constraints on values are part of the type
runs: Compiled ahead of time to machine code, with run-time checks for things like out-of-range values and no garbage collector required.
what: Ada was commissioned by the US Department of Defense to replace the hundreds of languages its projects were using with one language for large, long-lived, real-time systems. It is strict on purpose: the compiler checks types, ranges and task interactions so that errors show up before the software is in the field. A subset called SPARK goes further and lets tools prove mathematically that a program has no run-time errors.

name: Dafny
year_note: Microsoft Research lists the Dafny project as established in December 2008; the reference paper "Dafny: An Automatic Program Verifier for Functional Correctness" appeared at LPAR-16 in 2010
org: Microsoft Research originally; now developed as an open source project at dafny.org
typing: static
runs: The Dafny verifier translates the program and its specifications to the Boogie intermediate language and asks the Z3 solver to prove them; verified code is then compiled to C#, Java, JavaScript, Go or Python.
what: Dafny is a programming language with verification built in. Next to ordinary code you write what each method requires and guarantees, and a static verifier tries to prove, automatically and while you type, that the code meets those promises. It aims to make proving a program correct feel like getting it to compile.

notable.name: IronFleet
notable.text: Microsoft Research's Ironclad project used Dafny to verify the safety and liveness of practical distributed systems.

notable.name: AWS Encryption SDK for Dafny
notable.text: Amazon publishes an implementation of its client-side encryption library, the AWS Encryption SDK, in Dafny.

name: Solidity
year_note: Solidity was publicly previewed for the first time in November 2014 at Devcon0; version numbering in the codebase began in July 2015
designers: the Solidity team of the Ethereum project
typing: static
runs: The solc compiler turns Solidity into bytecode for the Ethereum Virtual Machine; the bytecode is stored on the blockchain and executed by every node of the network when the contract is called.
what: Solidity is a statically typed, curly-bracket language for writing smart contracts: programs that live on the Ethereum blockchain and control accounts and assets there. Once deployed, a contract runs inside a peer-to-peer network where nobody has special authority over its execution.

notable.name: Uniswap V2
notable.text: The core smart contracts of the Uniswap V2 decentralized exchange are written in Solidity.

notable.name: OpenZeppelin Contracts
notable.text: A widely used library of Solidity building blocks for secure smart contract development.
